sections.h2: What does a Ridgewood seller need to arrange first?
sections.html:
A Ridgewood seller needs a smoke detector and carbon monoxide certificate from the Fire Prevention Bureau before closing. The village Building Department does not issue a certificate of occupancy when a one or two family house is resold, so this single inspection is the main local gate.

Ridgewood is a Bergen County village about 20 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan. The Census Bureau counted 25,979 residents in 2020 and estimates 26,527 for July 2025. Its 5.74 square miles of land give it about 4,524 people per square mile, and 82.5 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied, so a typical sale here is a family home changing hands rather than a rental unit.

sections.h2: How much does a Ridgewood resale inspection cost, and when must it happen?
sections.html:
The fee depends on how far ahead of closing you book. The Fire Prevention Bureau charges per dwelling unit and appointments run Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. through the Inspection Office at 201-444-7898, extension 5480.

  • More than 10 days before closing: $120.
  • Fewer than 10 days before closing: $150.
  • Within 3 days of closing: $200.
  • An inspection completed after the closing adds a $500 penalty to the $200 fee, because state law requires the certificate before transfer.

Card payments are taken in person only and carry a 3 percent technology charge. Cash and checks payable to the Village of Ridgewood are accepted at the bureau, 201 East Glen Avenue. A house with a monitored central station alarm must also be registered with the Ridgewood Fire Department at 201-444-8822, extension 4112.

sections.h2: What is Ridgewood's history, and which houses have protected status?
sections.html:
Johannes Van Emburgh built the first house in 1700 on 250 acres he had bought two years earlier. The Village of Ridgewood was created on November 20, 1894, with the same boundaries as Ridgewood Township, and the village took over municipal government while the township stayed on as a school district. The village later gained land from Franklin Township in 1925, Washington Township in 1971 and Ho-Ho-Kus in 1974.

Several Dutch-era homes are on the National Register of Historic Places, among them the Ackerman houses on Doremus Avenue and Lincoln Avenue, the Archibald-Vroom House at 160 East Ridgewood Avenue and the Westervelt-Cameron House on East Glen Avenue, built around 1767. Ridgewood Station at Garber Square was added in 1984.

The village building page lists the Historic Preservation Commission among the bodies that may review exterior changes, so an owner of an older house should ask the Building Department whether any approval applies before listing a project as a selling point.

sections.h2: Which permits and village rules can slow a Ridgewood closing?
sections.html:
Ridgewood's building FAQ says replacing a furnace, boiler or water heater requires a permit, as does creating habitable space in a basement or attic, adding a bathroom or laundry room, and building a deck, generator pad or accessory structure. Pools, patios, driveways, sheds and fences need a zoning certificate first.

Painting, flooring, trim, and replacing a window or door in the same opening do not need permits. Permits expire if work does not start within 12 months, or if work is abandoned for 6 months.

  • A permit is also required to cut down a tree with a diameter of eight inches or more at breast height on private land, and trees in the public right-of-way belong to the village.
  • Sidewalk repair is the owner's job, and the village arborist assesses any shade tree whose roots lift the slab.
  • New Jersey allows an oil tank to be abandoned in place with a permit, but the village notes that lenders and insurers increasingly want a buried tank removed, which can matter at sale.

sections.h2: Which roads, trains and neighborhoods define Ridgewood?
sections.html:
Ridgewood has 94.70 miles of road, 79.79 of them municipal. Route 17 runs along the east side, Franklin Turnpike and County Route 84 (East and West Ridgewood Avenue) carry local traffic, and County Route 507 follows Maple Avenue.

The Ridgewood station has three platforms and is served by both the Main Line and the Bergen County Line, with trains to Hoboken and transfers at Secaucus Junction for New York Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 148, 163 and 164 go to Port Authority and the 175 to the George Washington Bridge; Short Line also runs along Route 17.

Neighborhood names buyers use include Downtown around East Ridgewood Avenue, Scrabbletown near Franklin Turnpike and East Glen Avenue, the Old Country Club by the Midland Park line, The View on the ridge off Crest Road, Upper Ridgewood, Salem Ridge, Floral Park, Brookside, The Lawns and The Heights, which developed between the 1890s and 1930.

sections.h2: Which schools and parks serve Ridgewood homes?
sections.html:
Ridgewood Public Schools run from prekindergarten to grade 12 with 10 schools and 5,613 students in 2020 to 2021. Six elementary schools cover kindergarten through grade 5, Benjamin Franklin and George Washington middle schools cover grades 6 to 8, and Ridgewood High School had 1,775 students. The state places the district in District Factor Group J, the highest of its eight categories.

Graydon Park has a pool, Veterans Field has four ball fields and a bandshell, Citizens Park sits across from George Washington Middle School, and the Wild Duck Pond is part of Saddle River County Park with a 6-mile path to Glen Rock, Fair Lawn, Paramus, Rochelle Park and Saddle Brook.

sections.h2: What do Bergen County appeals and closing costs look like for Ridgewood?
sections.html:
Bergen County takes assessment appeals through its Board of Taxation at Two Bergen County Plaza in Hackensack, 201-336-6300, and its page says the deadline for 2026 appeals has passed. Hearings come after the annual April 1 filing date. If an assessment tops $750,000, a Ridgewood owner may file directly with the Tax Court by April 1.

On a sale at the village's $891,200 median value, the state Realty Transfer Fee works out to about $8,313 when each band's rate is applied to the slice of price inside it. Above $1,000,000 a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller: 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000, which is $15,000 on a $1.5 million sale.

faqs.q: Does Ridgewood issue a certificate of occupancy at resale?
faqs.a: No. The village Building Department does not issue one for the resale of a one or two family house. A smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification from the Fire Prevention Bureau is required before closing.

faqs.q: What happens if the Ridgewood inspection is done after closing?
faqs.a: The owner pays a $500 penalty on top of the $200 certification fee. The schedule is $120 more than 10 days out, $150 inside 10 days and $200 inside 3 days.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remove a tree before selling in Ridgewood?
faqs.a: Yes for a qualifying tree, meaning one eight inches or wider at breast height on private land. Trees in the public right-of-way need consent from the village arborist.

faqs.q: Is a Ridgewood buyer likely to ask about water quality?
faqs.a: Some will. Ridgewood Water entered a consent order with the state in May 2023 to treat PFAS in its groundwater supply, with a stated goal of finishing treatment by the end of 2026. The utility publishes current test data.

faqs.q: How much is the transfer fee on a typical Ridgewood sale?
faqs.a: About $8,313 at the village's $891,200 median home value. The seller pays it when the deed is recorded, and sales over $1,000,000 add a percentage fee.
